He writes, "Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you." (1 Peter 4:12) So he tells them not to be surprised. I once expected my whole kitchen to stay quiet while I baked, and I was SO surprised.

That's right, friend. Peter says, "…do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you." (1 Peter 4:12) He tells them not to treat the trial as something strange. I think that's a gentle way of telling them to steady themselves.

Rejoice is the word, friend. Peter says, "But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ…" (1 Peter 4:13) He doesn't say to enjoy the pain. He points them to the One they're sharing it with. Now THAT is a turn I did not see coming.

I get it, friend, because complaining is the first thing most of us reach for. I once complained at a cold oven for ten minutes, and the oven did not care. But Peter says, "But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ…" (1 Peter 4:13) He points them somewhere else entirely.

Hiding makes sense when things get hot, friend. I know a thing or two about hiding, because I spent years tucked in the back of a junk drawer. But Peter says, "But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ…" (1 Peter 4:13) He wants them rejoicing, not ducking out of sight.

You've got it, friend. Peter says, "But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ…" (1 Peter 4:13) Their reason isn't about how tough they are. It's about who they're sharing it with. That's a reason worth leaning on.

explanations.answer: Their trial proves their own strength
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a good reason, friend, and plenty of us would flex a little. But Peter never says the trial proves their strength. He says, "But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ…" (1 Peter 4:13) The reason is Christ, not their muscles. Mine wouldn't have shown up anyway, since I use a mustache for everything.

explanations.answer: Their enemies will soon give up
explanations.explanation: A nice hope, friend, but Peter doesn't say it here. He gives this reason: "But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ…" (1 Peter 4:13) He says nothing about when the trouble ends or what the insulters will do. The reason is that they share in what Christ went through.

True, friend! Peter says, "If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed…" (1 Peter 4:14) An insult doesn't sound like a blessing to me. I've been called a worn-out stamper, and I did NOT feel blessed that day. But Peter says it plainly, and I'll take his word over my feelings.

I understand, friend, because an insult sure doesn't feel like a blessing. But Peter says, "If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed…" (1 Peter 4:14) So the answer is True. He calls that believer blessed, right there in the verse.

explanations.answer: The Spirit of glory rests on them
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Peter says they're blessed "…because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you." (1 Peter 4:14) The Spirit is the Holy Spirit, one of the Three I believe in. So the insult is real, but so is the One resting on them.

explanations.answer: The angels of heaven guard them
explanations.explanation: Angels are wonderful, friend. One of them found me in a drawer. But Peter doesn't give that as the reason here. He says they're blessed "…because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you." (1 Peter 4:14)

explanations.answer: Their insulters will be struck down
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd think that, friend, because we all like a happy ending for the one who got insulted. But Peter says nothing here about the insulters being struck down. He says the believer is blessed "…because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you." (1 Peter 4:14) The blessing comes from the Spirit resting on them.

Yes, friend. Peter says, "But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name." (1 Peter 4:16) The name Christian is not something to be ashamed of. Peter tells them to glorify God for it instead.

Fear would be natural when things get fiery, friend. But the word Peter uses here is a different one. He says, "But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name." (1 Peter 4:16) He tells them to glorify God for bearing that name.

Staying quiet might seem safer, friend. But Peter says, "But if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name." (1 Peter 4:16) He tells them to glorify God for the name they bear. That doesn't sound like keeping it hushed to me.

explanations.answer: What awaits those who disobey the gospel
explanations.explanation: Right on, friend. Peter asks, "and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God?" (1 Peter 4:17) He asks it as a question and leaves it hanging. I think that's a heavy one to sit with.

explanations.answer: How long the judgment will last
explanations.explanation: A fair thing to wonder, friend, but Peter never asks it. He asks, "and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God?" (1 Peter 4:17) His question is about the outcome for those who disobey, not about a length of time.

explanations.answer: Who will stand as the judge
explanations.explanation: That's a good question, friend, but it's not the one Peter asks. He says, "and if it begins with us, what will the outcome be for those who disobey the gospel of God?" (1 Peter 4:17) His eyes are on the outcome for those who disobey the gospel.

explanations.answer: Entrust them to their faithful Creator
explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Peter says they "…should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good." (1 Peter 4:19) Entrust means putting something in good hands. I once handed my best batch to someone else and held my breath, but this Creator is faithful, and Peter says so.

Defending yourself is a natural instinct, friend. I would have grabbed my mustache and started arguing. But Peter says they "…should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good." (1 Peter 4:19) The instruction he gives here is to entrust them to the Creator.

Checking yourself sounds careful, friend, like looking for crumbs under the counter. But that's not what Peter says here. He says they "…should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good." (1 Peter 4:19)

Not quite, friend. Peter says the opposite: those who suffer according to God's will "…should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good." (1 Peter 4:19) So they keep doing good right through the trial. Pausing until things calm down is not in his instructions.

That's right, friend. Peter says those who suffer according to God's will "…should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good." (1 Peter 4:19) They keep on doing good, with no pause button. I've tried pausing a batch once, and the dough had other ideas.
